outline: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. In ${}^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$, $x$ is the nucleon number (protons + neutrons) and $y$ the proton number, so neutrons $=x-y$ and, for an ion, electrons $=y-(\text{charge})$ (a $2-$ ion has $y+2$). Neutral atoms of isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration, so the same chemical properties; they have different numbers of neutrons, so different masses and densities.

misconceptions.statement: Atoms with the same mass (nucleon) number are isotopes of the same element.
misconceptions.refutation: Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so their nucleon numbers differ. Atoms with the same nucleon number but different proton numbers are atoms of different elements.
misconceptions.contrast: $^{40}\mathrm{Ar}$, $^{40}\mathrm{K}$ and $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ all have 40 nucleons but 18, 19 and 20 protons, so they are three different elements. $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ both have 17 protons and are isotopes.

misconceptions.statement: Isotopes differ in their numbers of protons or electrons, not neutrons.
misconceptions.refutation: The proton number defines the element, so isotopes of one element always share it. Only the number of neutrons changes. A neutral atom also has as many electrons as protons, so isotopes have equal electrons too.
misconceptions.contrast: $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$: 17 protons and 17 electrons each, but 18 and 20 neutrons. $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}^-$ differs from $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ only in electrons, so it is an ion, not an isotope.

misconceptions.statement: In a nuclear equation only one of the two numbers has to balance; a particle such as an electron can be ignored when balancing the mass number.
misconceptions.refutation: Both the nucleon numbers (top) and the proton numbers (bottom) must add up to the same totals on each side. An electron has nucleon number 0 and charge $-1$, so it cannot make up a missing nucleon.
misconceptions.contrast: For $^{32}\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{X}\to{}^{32}\mathrm{P}+{}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p}$ the missing particle needs nucleon number 1 and proton number 0, a neutron. An electron balances neither number, and a proton fixes the nucleon number but breaks the proton number.

misconceptions.statement: Isotopes with different numbers of neutrons must have different chemical properties.
misconceptions.refutation: Chemical properties depend on the electron arrangement, in particular the outer electrons, which decides how an atom gains, loses or shares electrons. Neutrons carry no charge and do not change the electron configuration.
misconceptions.contrast: $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ have the same configuration $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^2$ and form the same compounds with the same equations. They differ only in mass.

misconceptions.statement: Isotopes are the same element, so all their properties are identical, including mass and density.
misconceptions.refutation: Extra neutrons add mass, so isotopes have different atomic masses. Any physical property that depends on mass, such as the density of a sample, then differs slightly.
misconceptions.contrast: At the same temperature and pressure, $^{37}\mathrm{Cl_2}$ gas is denser than $^{35}\mathrm{Cl_2}$ gas, although both react chemically in the same way.

misconceptions.statement: The lower number in a nuclide symbol is the neutron number.
misconceptions.refutation: The lower number is the proton (atomic) number. The neutron number is the upper number minus the lower number.
misconceptions.contrast: $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ has 17 protons and $37-17=20$ neutrons, not 17 neutrons.

misconceptions.statement: Isotopes form different compounds because their neutron numbers differ.
misconceptions.refutation: Bonding uses electrons. Neutral isotopes have the same electron arrangement, so they form the same compounds with the same formulae; only the molar mass of the compound changes.
misconceptions.contrast: $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ both burn to give $\mathrm{CO}_2$; the $^{14}\mathrm{CO}_2$ molecules are simply heavier.

misconceptions.statement: Each isotope of an element has the same relative atomic mass.
misconceptions.refutation: Each isotope has its own mass. The relative atomic mass of an element is a weighted average over its isotopes.
misconceptions.contrast: Chlorine has $A_\mathrm{r}=35.5$, an average of $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$; no single chlorine atom has mass 35.5.

worked.problem: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$.

steps.why: The proton (atomic) number is the lower number; it identifies the element and ignores any charge.
The nucleon number counts protons plus neutrons, so subtract the protons. Students often use 37 as the neutron count.
The minus sign on $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ means one extra electron was gained; the charge changes the electrons only.

faded.problem: State the number of electrons in the ion $^{71}_{31}\mathrm{Ga}^{3+}$.

worked.problem: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$.

steps.why: The proton (atomic) number is the lower number; the charge does not change it.
The nucleon number counts protons plus neutrons, so subtract the protons; the charge does not change the nucleus.
The 2+ charge means two electrons were lost; a positive ion has fewer electrons than protons.

faded.problem: State the number of electrons in the ion $^{52}_{24}\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$.

items.stem: Which statement about the isotopes of an element is correct?

options.A: They have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
options.B: They have different numbers of protons and the same number of neutrons.
options.C: They have the same number of protons and neutrons but different numbers of electrons.
options.D: They have the same nucleon number but different proton numbers.

items.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so the proton number is fixed; they differ only in neutrons and therefore in nucleon number. The statement about the same nucleon number but different proton numbers describes atoms of different elements.
hints: Which particle count decides which element an atom belongs to?
Isotopes are all atoms of one element, so one of the particle counts must stay fixed and another must vary.
Test each option: would the two atoms it describes still be atoms of the same element?

items.stem: Define the term *isotope*.

rubric.point: same number of protons / same atomic (proton) number (atoms of the same element)
different number of neutrons (so different nucleon / mass number)

items.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Both halves are needed for full marks.
hints: A definition has to name particles, not just say 'different masses'.
State what stays the same and what changes, in terms of protons and neutrons.
Same number of ... but different number of ...

items.stem: An atom has nucleon number [[A]] and proton number [[Z]]. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
items.explanation: Nucleon number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = nucleon number − proton number.
hints: The nucleon number counts the particles in the nucleus.
Nucleon number is the total of protons and neutrons.
Subtract the proton number from the nucleon number.

items.stem: Which pair of species are isotopes of the same element?
items.explanation: Only the chlorine pair has the same proton number (17) with different neutron numbers (18 and 20). The argon and potassium pair has equal nucleon numbers but different elements, the chlorine atom and chloride ion differ only in electrons and the carbon and oxygen pair has the same number of neutrons (8) but different protons.
hints: Work out the protons and neutrons for each species, not just the top numbers.
For every pair, ask: same element (same proton number) and different neutron number?
Find the pair with equal bottom numbers and unequal top numbers, with no charge change.

items.stem:
Gallium (proton number 31) has two isotopes, $^{69}\mathrm{Ga}$ and $^{71}\mathrm{Ga}$.

(a) Define the term *isotope*.

(b) Give the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of each isotope.

scheme.point: isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons

items.explanation: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number: $69-31=38$ and $71-31=40$. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons (31).
hints: Start from the definition, then use the two nucleon numbers.
Neutrons come from nucleon number minus proton number; a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons.
Both isotopes share the same proton and electron numbers; only the neutron numbers differ.

items.stem: Atoms of $^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}$, $^{40}_{19}\mathrm{K}$ and $^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}$ are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.A: They have the same total number of protons and neutrons.
options.B: They have the same number of neutrons.
options.C: They have the same number of electrons.
options.D: They are isotopes of the same element.

items.explanation: All three have nucleon number 40. Their proton numbers (18, 19, 20) differ, so they are different elements with 22, 21 and 20 neutrons, so the statements about equal neutron numbers, equal electron numbers and being isotopes are wrong. Sharing a nucleon number does not make atoms isotopes.
hints: Read the top and bottom numbers of each symbol carefully.
Isotopes need the same proton number. Do these three have it?
For each option, work out that particle count for all three atoms before deciding.

items.stem:
Which statements are correct when referring to the two common isotopes of chlorine?

1. The isotopes have different masses.
2. The isotopes have different numbers of nucleons.
3. The isotopes have the same chemical reactions.
items.explanation: The two isotopes differ in neutrons, so they have different masses (1) and different nucleon numbers (2), yet the same electron configuration gives the same chemical reactions (3). Option B is wrong because statement 3 is also true: extra neutrons do not change the chemistry.
hints: Take each numbered statement on its own and decide true or false.
Think about which particles change between isotopes, and which particles control chemical reactions.
Neutrons change mass and nucleon number; electrons control reactions.

items.stem: An ion has nucleon number [[A]], proton number [[Z]] and charge [[q]]+. Calculate the number of electrons in the ion.
items.explanation: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. A positive ion has lost $q$ electrons, so electrons = proton number − charge. The nucleon number is not needed.
hints: Which particles does the charge on an ion change?
A positive charge means electrons have been lost from the neutral atom.
Start from the electron count of the neutral atom, then remove the number of positive charges.

items.stem: In the symbol $^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na}$, what do the two numbers show?

options.A: 23 is the nucleon (mass) number and 11 is the proton (atomic) number.
options.B: 23 is the proton number and 11 is the nucleon number.
options.C: 23 is the number of neutrons and 11 is the number of protons.
options.D: 23 is the number of protons and 11 is the number of neutrons.

items.explanation: In the notation ${}^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$ the top number $x$ is the nucleon (mass) number and the bottom number $y$ is the proton (atomic) number. Neutrons = $23-11=12$.
hints: One number is bigger than the other for a reason: which of them counts more particles?
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; one number counts both, the other counts only one type.
Ask which of the two numbers could include both kinds of particle in the nucleus.

items.stem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion $^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$?
items.explanation: Protons = 13 (bottom number). Neutrons = $27-13=14$. The charge of 3+ means three electrons lost from the neutral atom's 13, leaving 10. The wrong rows add electrons instead of removing them (16), use the nucleon number as the neutron count (27) or ignore the charge (13).
hints: Read off the protons from the symbol first, then handle neutrons and electrons separately.
Neutrons: nucleon number minus proton number. Electrons: think about what a positive charge tells you.
A 3+ ion has lost three electrons.

items.stem:
Complete the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons for each species:

| species | protons | neutrons | electrons |
|---|---|---|---|
| $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ | | | |
| $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ | | | |
| $^{16}_{8}\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ | | | |
items.explanation: Protons = bottom number; neutrons = top − bottom; electrons = protons − (charge), so a $2+$ ion has two fewer electrons than protons and a $2-$ ion has two more.
hints: Handle the columns in order: protons, neutrons, then electrons.
Protons and neutrons ignore the charge; only the electrons depend on it.
A negative charge means extra electrons; a positive charge means fewer than the protons.

items.stem: A single $^{32}\mathrm{P}$ nucleus can be produced when a single $^{32}\mathrm{S}$ nucleus joins with particle X. In the process a proton is emitted. What is particle X?
items.explanation: The products have total nucleon number $32+1=33$ and total proton number $15+1=16$. $^{32}\mathrm{S}$ has nucleon number 32 and proton number 16, so X has nucleon number 1 and proton number 0: a neutron. The commonly chosen B (electron) fails to balance the nucleon number, so it cannot make up the missing nucleon.
hints: Write the reaction as a nuclear equation with top and bottom numbers.
Balance the top numbers and the bottom numbers separately, remembering the emitted proton is a product.
Subtract the reactant totals from the product totals to get the nucleon number and proton number of X, then match them to a particle.

items.stem: The isotopes $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ have the same chemical properties. Explain why.

rubric.point: same number of electrons / same electron configuration
chemical properties depend on electrons (number/arrangement), which neutrons do not change

items.explanation: Chemical properties depend on the number and arrangement of electrons, especially the outer electrons. Neutral atoms of isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration, because they have the same number of protons.
hints: Ask which particles take part when atoms react.
Compare the electrons of the two isotopes, not their masses.
Link the proton number of each isotope to the number of electrons in its neutral atom, then say what controls reactions.

items.stem: Which property is the same for the isotopes $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$?
items.explanation: Both have 17 electrons in the same arrangement. Mass, neutron number and (since density depends on mass) density all differ.
hints: Decide which of the properties depend on the nucleus and which on the electrons.
The isotopes differ in their neutrons: cross out anything that depends on neutrons.
For each option, ask whether it would change if the nucleus gained two neutrons.

items.stem: Why do the isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?

options.A: They have the same number of electrons, giving the same electron configuration.
options.B: The extra neutrons take part in the bonding of the heavier isotope in the same way.
options.C: They have the same nucleon number.
options.D: They have the same number of neutrons.

items.explanation: Reactions involve electrons, and isotopes have identical electron configurations. Neutrons are not involved in bonding, and isotopes differ in nucleon number and neutron number.
hints: Which particles are transferred or shared in chemical reactions?
Consider what the isotopes share and whether that shared thing takes part in reactions.
It is not the nucleus; the shared feature is outside it.

items.stem: Samples of gaseous $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.A: They have the same chemical properties and the same density.
options.B: They have the same chemical properties but different densities.
options.C: They have different chemical properties but the same density.
options.D: They have different chemical properties and different densities.

items.explanation: Same electron configuration means the same chemical properties, and different neutron numbers give different molecular masses and so different densities of the gas at the same temperature and pressure.
hints: Split the question: one half about chemistry, one half about physical properties.
Chemistry depends on electrons; density depends on mass.
Check what is the same and what is different between the isotopes for each half.

items.stem: A student says that $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ must be more reactive than $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ because it has two extra neutrons. Explain why the student is wrong.

rubric.point: isotopes have the same number of electrons / electron configuration
neutrons have no charge / do not take part in chemical reactions

items.explanation: Neutral atoms of both isotopes have six protons and six electrons in the same configuration, and neutrons do not take part in reactions, so the chemical behaviour is the same.
hints: Which particles decide how an atom reacts?
Compare the number and arrangement of electrons in the two isotopes.
Say what the two extra neutrons do change, then check whether they change the particles involved in reactions.

items.stem:
Bromine has two isotopes, $^{79}\mathrm{Br}$ and $^{81}\mathrm{Br}$.

(a) Explain why the two isotopes have the same chemical properties.

(b) State one physical property that is different for the two isotopes and explain why.

scheme.point: same number of electrons / same electron configuration
chemical properties depend on the electrons (neutrons do not take part)
because the isotopes have different numbers of neutrons (81 Br has two more)

items.explanation: Chemistry depends on electrons, which are identical. Mass and density differ because $^{81}\mathrm{Br}$ has two more neutrons, so a heavier nucleus for essentially the same size.
hints: Answer (a) in terms of electrons and (b) in terms of neutrons.
For (b) name a physical property linked to mass, then trace it back to the nucleus.
In (b), link the difference in the nucleus to a quantity you could measure for a sample.

items.stem: At the same temperature and pressure, $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ gas is denser than $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ gas. What is the best explanation?

options.A: $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms have more protons than $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms.
options.B: Each $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ molecule has a greater mass, and equal volumes of the two gases contain equal numbers of molecules.
options.C: $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms have more electrons than $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms.
options.D: $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms have a different electron configuration, so they form stronger Cl–Cl bonds.

items.explanation: Each $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atom has two more neutrons, so each molecule is heavier, while equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold the same number of molecules; mass ÷ volume is therefore larger. The isotopes have the same proton number and the same electron configuration (the other three statements are false).
hints: Density is mass divided by volume. Which of these does the extra particle change?
Isotopes have the same numbers of protons and electrons, so cross out anything that changes those.
For the options left, check that the statement about mass and about volume are both true for gases at the same temperature and pressure.

items.stem: A diatomic gas consists of molecules $\mathrm{X_2}$ in which each atom has a molar mass of [[A]] g mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the density of the gas at r.t.p., in g dm$^{-3}$. Take the molar volume at r.t.p. as $24.0\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$.
items.explanation: One mole of $\mathrm{X_2}$ has mass $2A$ g and occupies 24.0 dm³, so density = mass ÷ volume. A heavier isotope gives a larger density.
hints: Density is mass divided by volume; use one mole of the gas.
The gas is diatomic, so a mole of molecules has twice the molar mass of an atom.
Divide the mass of one mole of molecules by the molar volume.

items.stem: Explain why isotopes of the same element have different masses.

rubric.point: different numbers of neutrons
each neutron adds mass (protons and neutrons make up the mass of the atom)

items.explanation: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, and neutrons contribute to the mass of the nucleus, so the atoms have different masses.
hints: Which particle count differs between isotopes?
Protons and neutrons make up almost all the mass of an atom.
More neutrons give a heavier atom.

items.stem: Which property is greater for $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ than for $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ at the same temperature and pressure?

options.A: the number of protons per molecule
options.B: the number of electrons per molecule

items.explanation: Each $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atom has two more neutrons, so a mole of molecules has a larger mass and the gas is denser. Protons, electrons and ion formation are identical.
hints: Which of these depends on mass, and which on protons and electrons?
The two gases differ only in the number of neutrons in the nuclei.
For each option, ask whether it would change if every nucleus gained two neutrons.

items.stem: Equal volumes of $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ are measured at the same temperature and pressure. Take the molar mass of each atom as equal to its nucleon number in g mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the ratio $\dfrac{\text{density of }{}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2}{\text{density of }{}^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2}$.
items.explanation: Equal volumes at the same T and p contain equal numbers of moles, so the density ratio equals the ratio of molar masses: $\dfrac{74}{70}=1.057$.
hints: Equal volumes of gas at the same T and p contain the same amount in moles.
So the density ratio is the ratio of the molar masses of the two molecules.
Molar mass of a diatomic molecule is twice that of an atom; put the heavier isotope on top.

items.stem:
Deuterium, $^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}$, is an isotope of hydrogen, $^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}$.

(a) State the number of neutrons in one atom of deuterium.

(b) Deuterium gas, $\mathrm{D_2}$, has a molar mass of $4.00\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate its density at r.t.p., in $\mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$. Take the molar volume at r.t.p. as $24.0\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$.

(c) Explain why $\mathrm{D_2}$ has the same chemical properties as $\mathrm{H_2}$ but a different density.

scheme.point: same number of electrons / same electron configuration, so same chemical properties
extra neutron gives a greater mass (per molecule), so a different (greater) density

items.explanation: Neutrons $=2-1=1$. Density $=4.00/24.0=0.167\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$. The isotopes have the same electrons (same chemistry) but different masses (different density).
hints: Part (a) uses nucleon number and proton number; part (b) is density = mass ÷ volume for one mole.
In (b) use one mole of D$_2$ and the molar volume at r.t.p., $24.0\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$.
For (c) contrast electrons with neutrons: which set is the same, and which set changes mass?

items.stem:
A single ³²P nucleus can be produced when a single ³²S nucleus joins with particle X. In the
process a proton is emitted.
What is particle X?

flashcards.back: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons / same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons (so different nucleon numbers).
No. They have the same nucleon number but different proton numbers (18 and 19), so they are different elements.

flashcards.front: In the symbol $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$, what are $x$ and $y$?
flashcards.back: $x$ is the nucleon (mass) number, the total of protons plus neutrons; $y$ is the proton (atomic) number.

flashcards.front: How do you find the numbers of neutrons and electrons in an ion from $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$ and its charge?
flashcards.back: Neutrons $=x-y$; electrons $=y-(\text{charge})$, so a $2+$ ion has $y-2$ electrons and a $2-$ ion has $y+2$.

flashcards.front: State and explain why isotopes have the same chemical properties.
flashcards.back: Neutral atoms of isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration; chemical properties depend on the electrons, not the neutrons.

flashcards.front: State and explain why isotopes have different physical properties (mass and density).
flashcards.back: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so different masses, and so different densities of the same substance.

9701-1.2.1.motivate: Two atoms can have different masses yet still be atoms of the same element. Which particle count decides whether they belong to that element?

discover.stem: The neutral atoms $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ are compared. Which pair of particle counts makes them isotopes?
discover.explanation: Both atoms have 17 protons. Their neutron counts are 18 and 20, respectively. Isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

9701-1.2.1.establish: **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The proton number identifies the element. Adding neutrons changes the nucleon number without changing the element. For $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$, both proton counts are 17; the neutron counts are $35-17=18$ and $37-17=20$. State both parts of the definition: same protons, different neutrons.
9701-1.2.1.connect: This definition builds on proton and nucleon number. Next, nuclide notation makes the two counts visible in one symbol.
9701-1.2.1.note:
- Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
- $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ both have 17 protons, but have 18 and 20 neutrons.
- Different nucleon number alone does not define isotopes; check that proton number is the same.
9701-1.2.1.self_explain: Why are $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ isotopes? Name both particle counts.
9701-1.2.1.plain_words: An isotope is an atom of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. The proton number fixes the element, so only the neutron count, and therefore the nucleon number, can vary. Equal nucleon numbers alone do not make isotopes.

terms.meaning: Atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
terms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 1.2 (bundle); SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2

terms.meaning: The number of protons in the nucleus; it fixes the element.
terms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 1.2 (bundle); SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2

terms.meaning: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
terms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 1.2 (bundle); SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2

terms.meaning: The number of neutrons: nucleon number minus proton number.
terms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 1.2 (bundle); SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2

forms.name: Define isotope
wordings: State what is meant by isotopes.
Explain what makes two atoms isotopes of each other.
forms.example:
- Both atoms have $17$ protons, so both are chlorine.
- Neutrons: $35-17=18$ and $37-17=20$, so the neutron numbers differ.
- Definition: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
forms.check: $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$ and $^{24}_{11}\mathrm{Na}$ both have nucleon number 24. Are they isotopes? Give a reason.
forms.answer: No. Their proton numbers are 12 and 11, so they are atoms of different elements. Equal nucleon numbers do not make isotopes.
forms.source: SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2; TQ 9701 c1.3 p.11 (define isotope)

rubric.point: Says they are not isotopes.
Gives different proton numbers, 12 and 11, so they are different elements.

retry.check: $^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$ are atoms of carbon. State the protons and neutrons in each, then say whether they are isotopes.
retry.answer: Both have 6 protons. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8. The proton numbers are the same and the neutron numbers differ, so they are isotopes.

rubric.point: Gives 6 protons in both atoms.
Gives 6 neutrons for carbon-12 and 8 for carbon-14.
Concludes they are isotopes because the proton number is the same.

misconceptions.idea: Atoms with the same mass (nucleon) number are isotopes of the same element.
misconceptions.temptation: Two atoms with the same nucleon number look like the same kind of atom.
misconceptions.fix: Check the proton number first. Equal nucleon numbers can belong to different elements, as with Mg-24 and Na-24.

misconceptions.idea: Isotopes differ in their numbers of protons or electrons, not neutrons.
misconceptions.temptation: A heavier isotope seems to have a different number of electrons too.
misconceptions.fix: Only the neutron number changes. A neutral isotope has as many electrons as protons, so isotopes have equal electrons.

diagram_descriptions: Three hydrogen isotopes, each labelled with protons, neutrons and electrons. Each atom has one proton and one electron; only the neutron count changes.
source_gaps: The definition is taken from the notes and the TQ 9701 question set; no examiner report on the isotope definition was read in this pass.

guided_discover.stem: Neutral atoms of boron-10 and boron-11 are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.A: They have different numbers of protons.
options.B: They have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
options.C: They have different numbers of electrons.
options.D: They have the same number of neutrons.

guided_discover.explanation: Boron has proton number 5, so both atoms have 5 protons and 5 electrons. The neutron numbers are $10-5=5$ and $11-5=6$, so the atoms are isotopes.

9701-1.2.2.motivate: A nuclide symbol carries enough information to count the particles in its nucleus. Reading the two numbers in the right places avoids mixing up elements and isotopes.

discover.stem: In $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$, what do the upper and lower numbers represent?

options.A: Upper: proton number; lower: neutron number
options.B: Upper: nucleon number; lower: proton number
options.C: Upper: neutron number; lower: electron number
options.D: Upper: nucleon number; lower: neutron number

discover.explanation: The upper 37 counts all nucleons, protons plus neutrons. The lower 17 counts protons; subtracting gives $37-17=20$ neutrons.

9701-1.2.2.establish: In $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$, the upper number $x$ is the **mass or nucleon number**, the total number of protons and neutrons. The lower number $y$ is the **atomic or proton number**, the number of protons. Therefore neutrons $=x-y$. In $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$, there are 17 protons and 20 neutrons. The element symbol is fixed by the proton number, so isotopes of chlorine all have 17 at the bottom.
9701-1.2.2.connect: The shared lower number shows why two atoms are the same element; different upper numbers show the neutron difference. This also supports particle counting in ions.
9701-1.2.2.note:
- In $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$, $x$ is nucleon (mass) number: protons plus neutrons.
- $y$ is proton (atomic) number: the number of protons.
- Neutrons $=x-y$; $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ has $37-17=20$ neutrons.
- An isotope differs in neutrons; an ion differs in electrons. Charge never changes the proton or neutron count.
9701-1.2.2.self_explain: Explain how the top and bottom numbers of $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ tell you its proton and neutron counts.
9701-1.2.2.plain_words: In $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$, the top number $x$ is the nucleon number and the bottom number $y$ is the proton number. Read the bottom number first to identify the element. Neutrons are $x-y$, and a neutral atom has $y$ electrons.

forms.name: Read particle counts from nuclide notation
wordings: State the number of protons and neutrons in this isotope.
Give the proton, neutron and electron numbers of this atom.
forms.example:
For $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$:
- Protons $=17$, the lower number.
- Nucleons $=37$, the upper number.
- Neutrons $=37-17=20$.
forms.check: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of $^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$.
forms.answer: Protons 26 (lower number). Neutrons $56-26=30$. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so 26 electrons.
forms.source: SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.2 (general chemical symbol); 9701 2020-2025 Paper 2.pdf p.159 (answer to 9701/21 Summer 2022 Q1(d)(i))

rubric.point: Gives 26 protons from the lower number.
Gives 30 neutrons as 56 minus 26.
Gives 26 electrons for the neutral atom.

retry.check: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion $^{81}_{35}\mathrm{Br}^{-}$.
retry.answer: Protons 35 (lower number). Neutrons $81-35=46$. The 1- charge means one extra electron, so electrons $=35+1=36$.

rubric.point: Gives 35 protons.
Gives 46 neutrons as 81 minus 35.
Gives 36 electrons, one more than the protons, for the 1- ion.

forms.name: Find the missing particle in a nuclear equation
wordings: Identify the missing particle X in this nuclear equation.
Deduce the identity of particle X, giving its nucleon and proton numbers.
forms.example:
$^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\to{}^{17}_{8}\mathrm{O}+\mathrm{X}$
- Nucleon numbers: $14+4=18=17+x$, so $x=1$.
- Proton numbers: $7+2=9=8+y$, so $y=1$.
- Nucleon number 1 and proton number 1 is a proton, $^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p}$.
forms.answer: Nucleon numbers: $10+1=11=7+x$, so $x=4$. Proton numbers: $5+0=5=3+y$, so $y=2$. X is an alpha particle, $^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.
forms.source: Pattern of ER 9701 w20 P11 Q3, as cited in pack misconception m3 (not re-read in this pass)

rubric.point: Balances nucleon numbers and finds 4.
Balances proton numbers and finds 2.
Identifies X as an alpha particle or helium-4.

retry.answer: Nucleon numbers: $24=24+x$, so $x=0$. Proton numbers: $11=12+y$, so $y=-1$. X is an electron, $^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$.

rubric.point: Balances nucleon numbers and finds 0.
Balances proton numbers and finds -1.
Identifies X as an electron.

misconceptions.idea: In a nuclear equation only one of the two numbers has to balance; a particle such as an electron can be ignored when balancing the mass number.
misconceptions.temptation: Electrons are so light that they can be left out of a nuclear balance.
misconceptions.fix: Balance the nucleon numbers and the proton numbers separately. An electron has nucleon number 0 and charge -1, so it cannot fill a nucleon gap.

misconceptions.idea: The lower number in a nuclide symbol is the neutron number.
misconceptions.temptation: The lower number looks like a count of the smaller particles, so it seems to be neutrons.
misconceptions.fix: The lower number y is the proton (atomic) number. The neutron number is x minus y, so $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ has 20 neutrons, not 17.

9701-1.2.3.motivate: Chlorine atoms with different neutron counts still take part in the same chemical reactions. What stays the same in the part of the atom that forms bonds?

discover.stem: Neutral $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms differ in neutrons. Why do they have the same chemical properties?

options.B: They have the same neutron number.
options.C: They have the same electron configuration.

discover.explanation: Both neutral atoms have 17 protons and 17 electrons, so their electron configurations are the same. Chemical reactions depend on electrons, while their different neutron counts change mass.

9701-1.2.3.establish: Isotopes of the same element have the same proton number. Neutral atoms of those isotopes therefore have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration. Chemical reactions involve electrons, especially outer electrons, so the isotopes have the **same chemical properties**. Their neutron counts differ, but neutrons do not take part in ordinary chemical reactions. An explanation needs both the unchanged electron configuration and its link to chemical behaviour.
9701-1.2.3.connect: The isotope definition gives the same proton number; this fixes the electron count of neutral atoms. The different neutron counts instead affect mass and density.
9701-1.2.3.note:
- Neutral isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration.
- Chemical reactions depend on electrons, so isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties.
- Different neutron counts do not change the electron configuration.
9701-1.2.3.self_explain: Explain why two neutral isotopes of chlorine react in the same way even though their nuclei contain different numbers of neutrons.
9701-1.2.3.plain_words: Chemical reactions involve electrons, especially the outer ones. Isotopes of one element have the same proton number, so neutral isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same arrangement. Neutrons carry no charge and do not change bonding.

forms.name: Explain identical chemical properties
wordings: Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
Explain why both isotopes of potassium have the same chemical properties.
Explain why isotopes react in the same way.
forms.example:
- Neutral $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atoms each have $17$ electrons.
- Both have the same electron arrangement, $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^5$.
- Reactions use the outer electrons, which are the same; neutrons carry no charge and take no part.
forms.check: Potassium-39 and potassium-41 both form $\mathrm{K}^+$ ions. Explain why they form the same ion.
forms.answer: Both neutral atoms have 19 electrons with the same arrangement, $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^1$. Each loses the outer $4s$ electron, so the same ion forms. The extra neutrons do not change the electrons.
forms.source: TQ 9701 c1.3 p.11 (explain identical chemical properties); 9701 2020-2025 Paper 2.pdf p.18 (potassium isotopes with the same chemical properties)

rubric.point: Both isotopes have the same number of electrons, equal to the protons when neutral.
The electron arrangement is the same, so the outer electrons match.
Neutrons do not change the electrons or bonding.

retry.check: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both form carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO}_2$. Explain why they form the same compound.
retry.answer: Both neutral atoms have 6 electrons with configuration $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^2$. The outer 2s and 2p electrons form the same bonds in $\mathrm{CO}_2$. The extra neutrons take no part in bonding.

rubric.point: Both atoms have 6 electrons.
The outer electrons form the same bonds.
Neutrons do not take part in bonding.

misconceptions.idea: Isotopes with different numbers of neutrons must have different chemical properties.
misconceptions.temptation: Heavier isotopes seem to react differently because their masses differ.
misconceptions.fix: Chemical properties depend on the outer electrons, which are the same. Neutrons carry no charge and do not change the electron configuration.

misconceptions.idea: Isotopes form different compounds because their neutron numbers differ.
misconceptions.temptation: Neutrons are part of the atom that bonds, so changing them seems to change which compounds form.
misconceptions.fix: Bonding uses electrons. Neutral isotopes have the same electron arrangement, so they form the same compounds with the same formulae; only the molar mass of the compound changes.

diagram_descriptions: Labelled isotopes of hydrogen: the electron count and arrangement are the same in each, while the neutron count changes.
source_gaps: The notes say chemical properties depend on the electron arrangement but do not discuss isotopes whose reaction rates differ; that is outside the 1.2.3 statement and is not taught here.

The exact Cambridge mark-scheme phrasing for the same-chemical-properties point was not obtained; a web search found only the syllabus wording, so the rubric follows pack misconception m4 and the notes (SaveMyExams 9701 c1.2 p.3).

9701-1.2.4.motivate: Two samples made from different isotopes can react alike yet have different masses for the same number of atoms. What measurable property of the samples might change?

discover.stem: A sample of $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ is compared with the same amount of $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ at the same conditions. Which property changes because of the neutron difference?
discover.explanation: Each $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ atom has two more neutrons and a greater mass. For equal amounts under the same conditions, this gives greater mass and density, while proton and electron counts are unchanged.

9701-1.2.4.establish: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, and neutrons contribute to atomic mass. Their atoms therefore have **different masses**. A sample made from the heavier isotope has more mass for the same number of atoms; under comparable conditions this gives a **different density**. These are the physical properties required here. Keep the cause explicit: different neutron count $\to$ different mass $\to$ different density.
9701-1.2.4.connect: The same electrons explain matching chemical properties; the different neutrons explain different masses and densities. State each reason with its own particle.
9701-1.2.4.note:
- Different neutron numbers give isotopes different atomic masses.
- Different mass can give samples different densities under comparable conditions.
- Link the physical difference to neutrons; link the chemical similarity to electrons.
9701-1.2.4.self_explain: Explain why $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ is denser than $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ at the same temperature and pressure.
9701-1.2.4.plain_words: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so their atoms have different masses. A sample of a heavier isotope has more mass for the same number of atoms, so under the same conditions it can have a different density. Physical properties that depend on mass can therefore differ.

forms.name: Explain a density difference between isotopes
wordings: Explain why isotopes have different densities.
Explain why samples of two isotopes differ in density.
Explain which of two isotopic gases is denser.
forms.example:
- $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ has molar mass $\approx 70\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$; $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ has $\approx 74\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
- At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules.
- So the $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}_2$ sample has more mass per volume and is denser. The extra neutrons cause the mass difference.
forms.check: $^{20}\mathrm{Ne}$ gas and $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}$ gas are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which is denser, and why? Answer in terms of the particles in each atom.
forms.answer: $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}$ is denser. Equal volumes contain equal numbers of atoms at the same temperature and pressure. Each $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}$ atom has two more neutrons, so the sample has more mass per volume.
forms.source: SaveMyExams notes 9701 c1.2 p.3-4 (physical properties: different mass and slight differences in density)

rubric.point: Identifies the 22 isotope as denser.
Links the difference to the extra neutrons adding mass.
States that equal volumes hold equal numbers of particles at the same conditions.

retry.check: Argon-36 and argon-40 gases are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which is denser, and why? Answer in terms of the particles in each atom.
retry.answer: Argon-40 is denser. At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes contain equal numbers of atoms. Each argon-40 atom has four more neutrons, so its sample has more mass per volume.

rubric.point: Identifies argon-40 as denser.
Links the difference to the extra neutrons adding mass.
States that equal volumes hold equal numbers of atoms at the same conditions.

misconceptions.idea: Isotopes are the same element, so all their properties are identical, including mass and density.
misconceptions.temptation: Two isotopes are the same element, so they should weigh the same.
misconceptions.fix: Extra neutrons add mass, so isotopes have different atomic masses. A property that depends on mass, such as the density of a sample, then differs slightly.

misconceptions.idea: Each isotope of an element has the same relative atomic mass.
misconceptions.temptation: The periodic table gives one mass for chlorine, so every chlorine atom should have that mass.
misconceptions.fix: Each isotope has its own mass. The relative atomic mass of chlorine, 35.5, is a weighted average of the $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ isotopes.

guided_discover.explanation: Both atoms have 3 protons and 3 electrons with the same configuration. Lithium-7 has one more neutron, so each atom has a greater mass.
